Filling an Array with 0s and 1s, and Counting

CountingLogic
Game: Fill a grid with 0s and 1s. Count the 1s in every row and every column. Try to get as many different counts as you can.
How to play: Press a square to change a 0 into a 1 and back. The counts show on the right and at the bottom, and the different ones are collected underneath.

Look for the math

The problem was set at the 1993–94 St. Petersburg Regional Olympiad for a 10 by 19 array: fill an N by M array with 0s and 1s, count the 1s in every row and column, and ask how many different counts there can be.

An easy upper bound

Swapping two rows or two columns changes none of the counts, so only the pattern of 1s matters, not where it sits. Say N ≥ M. A count is a whole number from 0 to N and no more, so there are at most N + 1 different ones. The test tried every array on boards of up to 20 squares and none went above max(N, M) + 1.

When the bound is reached

The page says N + 1 different counts can be had when N = M, when N = M + 1 and M > 2, when N is even and M ≥ N/2 + 1, and when N is odd and M > (N + 1)/2. The button builds such an array for every size from 2 by 2 to 20 by 20 where this holds: a few full rows, then a run of rows that grows shorter by one each time. The test also found that on every board up to 7 by 7 these are exactly the sizes where the bound is reached: for example 3 by 2 only gets 3 different counts, not 4, and 6 by 3 gets 6, not 7. That uses the Gale–Ryser theorem, which says exactly which lists of row counts and column counts some array can have.

Complements

Replacing every 0 by 1 and every 1 by 0 turns a count s into N - s in the columns and M - s in the rows. For a square array that sends the set {0, 1, ..., N} to itself, so the complement of an optimal array is optimal. That is what the Complement button shows.

Make a 4 by 4 array with five different counts, then press Complement. Then try 4 by 2: what is the most you can get?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
